intro: Apple's new AI-focused Mac hardware and OpenAI's custom Jalapeño inference chip dominated the conversation today, signaling that the race to own the full AI compute stack — from silicon to software — is heating up fast.

stories.title: OpenAI's Jalapeño Custom Chip Outperforms Nvidia Blackwell on AI Inference
stories.summary: OpenAI has published first results for Jalapeño, its custom inference chip, and the numbers are eye-catching: the company claims it delivers faster throughput and lower latency than Nvidia's Blackwell hardware for modern model inference. This is a significant milestone because it marks OpenAI's serious entry into the silicon game, a move that mirrors what Google did with TPUs years ago. The SemiAnalysis newsletter, which is generally rigorous about chip benchmarking, corroborated the claims and provided additional technical depth. For OpenAI, building its own silicon means lower cost-per-token at scale and reduced dependence on Nvidia — a vendor relationship that has become increasingly expensive and geopolitically complicated. For Nvidia, this is a signal that its largest customers are serious about vertical integration. The timing matters: OpenAI's CFO Sarah Friar simultaneously published a piece about the 'full stack behind abundant intelligence,' framing chips, compute, models, and products as a compounding system. Jalapeño is described as optimized specifically for inference (not training), which aligns with where most of the real-world compute spend is going as AI deployment scales. It's worth noting that 'industry-leading' benchmark claims from a company about its own chip should always be read with some skepticism until independent verification arrives. That said, the architectural direction — custom silicon for inference efficiency — is clearly the right bet. This is one of the more consequential hardware stories of the year and worth watching closely as more third-party analysis rolls in.

stories.title: OpenAI Disrupts Russian Covert Influence Operation Using AI-Generated Content
stories.summary: OpenAI announced it has banned a cluster of Russia-origin accounts that were using its models to run a covert influence campaign. The operation involved promoting a fake Israel-based think tank and producing content for a so-called 'sovereignty index' that praised Russia and criticized Western governments. This is notable because it's a concrete, documented case of AI being weaponized for disinformation at scale — not a hypothetical. OpenAI says it detected and disrupted the campaign, though the company is careful not to overstate how much of the operation it caught versus how much may still be running elsewhere. The fake think tank angle is particularly sophisticated: it lends apparent credibility to the content by routing it through a plausible-seeming third-party institution. This pattern — using AI to generate the volume of content needed to sustain a fake organization's public presence — is likely to become more common. OpenAI's transparency in publishing these disruption reports is genuinely useful; it gives researchers and policymakers a window into actual misuse patterns. The report also underscores that the threat isn't just deepfakes or voice cloning — it's the mundane, industrial-scale production of plausible text. For developers building on top of these models, it's a reminder that abuse detection and attribution are unsolved problems. Worth reading alongside the broader conversation about AI and the 2026 US midterms.

stories.title: Anthropic's Claude Cowork Gets Shared Memory Across Chat and Workspace
stories.summary: Anthropic has shipped a meaningful quality-of-life update to Claude: the AI now shares memory across its chat interface and the Cowork collaborative workspace, so users no longer have to re-explain their projects, preferences, and context every time they switch between the two surfaces. This sounds like a small thing but in practice it's one of the most persistent friction points in working with AI assistants — the fact that each session starts from zero. The update positions Claude Cowork as a more serious productivity tool rather than just a chat interface with a fancy sidebar. It also puts pressure on competitors: OpenAI's ChatGPT Work has similar memory features, and the differentiation between these products is increasingly about how well they maintain context across long-running, multi-session work. For power users who use Claude daily across different tasks, this should meaningfully reduce the 'briefing tax' they pay at the start of each interaction. The implementation details matter here — how long memory persists, what gets remembered versus forgotten, and whether users have granular control — and Anthropic hasn't been fully transparent about all of these. There's also a separate data point from the FT (via Simon Willison's blog) suggesting Anthropic's annualized revenue hit $65B in July, up from $47B in May, which is extraordinary growth. Yet the FT story also notes that Claude's best model is struggling to attract users relative to cheaper alternatives, which makes features like cross-surface memory more important for retention. Anthropic is clearly betting that a better integrated experience keeps users from defecting to cheaper models for everyday tasks.

stories.title: MIT Study: Using AI Chatbots for News Makes People Worse at Spotting Misinformation
stories.summary: A study from Pattie Maes's group at the MIT Media Lab has a finding that should give pause to anyone who relies on AI chatbots to stay informed: participants who used AI to evaluate news headlines over four weeks became measurably worse at detecting misinformation. Specifically, people who initially evaluated paired headlines and images were 21% more accurate at telling truth from falsehood at the start of the study — but that accuracy degraded over time for those relying on AI summaries. The mechanism appears to be cognitive offloading: when the AI does the critical evaluation work, users stop doing it themselves, and the skill atrophies. This is distinct from the question of whether the AI itself produces accurate summaries — even if the AI is right most of the time, users who defer to it may become less capable of independent judgment. The finding has obvious implications for AI-powered news digest products (yes, including ones like this), and for the broader deployment of AI as an information intermediary. It's also consistent with what researchers have found about GPS and spatial navigation — tools that do the work for you can reduce your ability to do that work yourself. For engineers building AI-assisted reading or research tools, this is a design challenge: how do you preserve user agency and critical thinking while still providing value? The study doesn't argue AI news tools are net negative, but it does argue they need to be designed with this risk in mind. Maes's lab has a track record of rigorous work on human-computer interaction, so this result deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed.

stories.title: Australia Bans AI-Generated Songs from Music Charts
stories.summary: Australia's music chart authority has announced that songs created by AI will be barred from official chart eligibility, a decision that came weeks after a DJ admitted to using AI to remix a Madonna track that topped the Australian charts. The move is one of the more concrete regulatory responses to AI-generated music anywhere in the world, and it sets a precedent that other markets may follow or explicitly reject. The immediate trigger — an AI remix topping the charts — highlights how quickly AI-generated content can reach mainstream audiences when the quality bar is cleared. The ban raises genuinely hard definitional questions: what counts as 'AI-generated' when most professional music production now uses AI tools for mixing, mastering, and even melody suggestion? Drawing the line between AI-assisted and AI-generated is a problem that has plagued policy discussions in visual art as well. For artists and rights holders, the chart ban is largely symbolic but symbolically important — it signals that institutional gatekeepers are taking a position. For AI music startups like Suno and Udio (and Google's Lyria, which just released version 3.5), this is a data point about where regulatory headwinds may blow. The practical enforcement challenge is substantial: chart authorities don't have reliable technical tools to detect AI generation in audio, and the DJ in the triggering incident self-disclosed. It's a policy that sets an intention more than it solves the problem, but intentions matter when they shape industry norms.

stories.title: AI Won't Replace Radiologists, But It Is Fundamentally Reshaping Their Work
stories.summary: Ars Technica has a thoughtful long-read on how AI is actually playing out in radiology — the specialty that became shorthand for 'AI will eliminate this profession' after Geoffrey Hinton's famous 2016 prediction that radiologists would be obsolete within five years. Ten years later, radiologists still exist and are still in demand, but their work is changing in ways that are worth understanding. AI systems are now routinely handling triage — flagging urgent cases, prioritizing worklists, and pre-screening for obvious findings — which means radiologists are spending more of their time on complex, ambiguous cases. The workflow change is real and significant: a radiologist today is more likely to be reviewing AI-flagged cases and providing clinical judgment than methodically working through a stack of scans. This has quality implications that cut both ways — AI can catch things humans miss, but radiologists may also be anchored by AI outputs, a phenomenon called automation bias. The piece notes that the 'AI replaces radiologist' framing was always too simple; the more accurate frame is 'AI replaces some tasks radiologists do.' For medical AI developers, the practical lesson is that the bottleneck isn't detection accuracy anymore — it's workflow integration, liability frameworks, and trust-building with clinicians. The story is a useful corrective to both the doom-and-gloom displacement narrative and the naive 'AI is just a tool' dismissal.

stories.title: Apple's New Mac Studio and Mac Mini Are Explicitly Designed for Local AI Inference
stories.summary: Apple refreshed both the Mac Studio (now with M5 Max and M5 Ultra) and the Mac Mini (now with M6 and M5 Pro) yesterday, and the framing is notably different from past hardware launches: Apple is positioning these machines explicitly as local AI inference platforms, not just desktop computers. The Mac Studio in particular has been popular among developers and researchers who daisy-chain multiple units to run large language models locally, and the new hardware refresh was designed with that use case in mind — better interconnect, more unified memory, and significantly higher AI compute throughput. The M6 chip in the Mac Mini brings a new neural engine architecture that Apple claims delivers substantially better performance per watt for inference workloads. The Mac Mini's price has gone up by $200, which will sting for budget-conscious buyers but reflects the upgraded silicon. For the AI developer community, the appeal of Apple Silicon for local inference has always been the unified memory architecture — you can run much larger models than a comparable GPU-equipped system because you're not constrained by VRAM. The M5 Ultra in the Mac Studio reportedly supports configurations with enough unified memory to run 70B+ parameter models at reasonable speeds. This is a genuine differentiator from x86 Windows machines, where you'd need a high-end Nvidia GPU (and its associated VRAM limits) to do comparable work. For engineers who want to run models locally for privacy, cost, or latency reasons, these machines represent a meaningful step up. The Hacker News thread on the M6/M5 Ultra announcement hit over 1,000 points, which is a reliable signal of genuine developer interest.

stories.title: FDA Authorizes First Wearable Device That Simultaneously Monitors Ketones and Blood Sugar
stories.summary: The FDA has authorized a wearable device that can continuously monitor both ketone levels and blood glucose simultaneously — a first in the consumer health sensor space. Current continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) track blood sugar but not ketones, so people managing diabetes or following ketogenic diets have had to use separate fingerprick tests for ketone measurement. A combined sensor that does both continuously and non-invasively is a meaningful clinical upgrade. The device is particularly relevant for people with Type 1 diabetes, where ketone levels can signal the onset of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening complication — catching it earlier through continuous monitoring rather than periodic testing could genuinely save lives. It also opens up interesting possibilities for metabolic health monitoring more broadly, as ketone tracking has become popular among people interested in longevity and metabolic optimization. The technical challenge of doing both measurements from a single wearable sensor is non-trivial; glucose and ketone sensing require different electrochemical approaches. The FDA authorization means the device has cleared the evidentiary bar for safety and efficacy, which is a meaningful signal of robustness. We don't have the brand name or full technical specs in the available source, but the Hacker News community scored this highly (323 points), suggesting it's a genuinely notable development. Watch for this to become a standard feature in next-generation health wearables from Apple, Dexcom, and Abbott.

stories.title: SpaceX Plans $100 Billion Second Starbase Spaceport in Louisiana
stories.summary: SpaceX has announced plans to build a second Starbase facility in Louisiana, with an investment commitment of up to $100 billion — a staggering figure that would make it one of the largest private infrastructure projects in American history. Construction is slated to begin in 2027, with a first Starship launch from the site targeted for as early as 2029. The announcement comes alongside news that the original Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas — currently the world's busiest spaceport — is about to slow down significantly as Starship operations shift toward Florida and eventually Louisiana. The Louisiana site is being described as a purpose-built, large-scale launch facility rather than an adaptation of existing infrastructure, which is why the investment figure is so large. For SpaceX, a second Starbase dramatically increases launch cadence capacity and reduces single-point-of-failure risk; if Boca Chica is grounded by regulatory issues or a mishap, operations could continue elsewhere. The choice of Louisiana is likely influenced by political considerations — it's a state with a favorable regulatory environment and congressional allies — as well as practical factors like coastal access and available land. The $100B figure should be read as a ceiling over many years rather than an immediate commitment; large infrastructure announcements routinely use headline numbers that cover multi-decade buildouts. Still, even at a fraction of that investment, this would be a transformational project for the region. It signals that SpaceX sees Starship as a multi-decade, multi-site operation rather than a single-facility experiment.

stories.title: Robotics Startup Generalist Hits $3B Valuation After Rapid Series Extension
stories.summary: Generalist, a physical AI and robotics startup, has reached a $3 billion valuation after raising a $200 million extension round — notably, this comes just months after it was valued at $2 billion, meaning it added a billion dollars in valuation in a matter of months. The speed of this re-rating is a signal of how hot the physical AI and humanoid robotics investment environment remains heading into late 2026. Generalist's pitch is around 'generalist' robots — systems that can perform a wide range of physical tasks rather than being purpose-built for one industrial application. This is the hard problem in robotics: most deployed robots are highly specialized, and building systems that generalize across tasks is where the interesting research and capital is flowing right now. The timing is interesting given the humanoid robot games in China (also in today's news) showing both impressive progress and spectacular failures — the sector is in a high-energy, high-volatility phase. For context, OpenAI's investment in Figure AI and Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics work are both pushing in similar directions, so Generalist is operating in an increasingly crowded field. The $200M extension suggests investors believe Generalist has a differentiated technical approach, though without more detail on what that is, the valuation jump is hard to fully evaluate. Physical AI is one of the few areas where the gap between demo and deployment remains genuinely wide, which cuts both ways for investors.

stories.title: OpenAI Loses Top Data Center Executive as Leadership Churn Continues
stories.summary: OpenAI has lost another senior executive — this time its head of data center operations — in what has become a notable and sustained pattern of high-profile departures over the past year. The executive in question had already been through an organizational reshuffle, with their reporting line shifted away from President Greg Brockman and placed under VP Sachin Katti, who now leads the infrastructure group. Whether the reporting change precipitated the departure or was coincidental isn't clear from the reporting. What is clear is that OpenAI's infrastructure organization — the team responsible for the compute backbone that runs its models — has been in flux at a moment when getting data center strategy right is existential for the company. OpenAI has made enormous bets on data center capacity through its Stargate partnership with Microsoft, SoftBank, and others, and losing operational leadership during that buildout is not ideal timing. The broader pattern of departures — including co-founders and senior research leaders over the past two years — raises legitimate questions about organizational stability and culture. OpenAI has continued to ship impressive products despite the churn, which suggests the organization is more resilient than the headlines imply, but the cumulative brain drain is worth tracking. For anyone building on the OpenAI API or making long-term bets on the platform, leadership stability is a relevant risk factor. Greg Brockman's reduced role in the infrastructure chain is also an interesting signal about how power and responsibility are being redistributed inside the company.

stories.title: Stability AI Raises $76M in Fresh Funding, Bringing Total to $232M
stories.summary: Stability AI, the maker of Stable Diffusion, has raised another $76 million in fresh funding, bringing its total raised to $232 million. This is a company that has had a genuinely turbulent few years — its founder Emad Mostaque departed in 2024 amid governance controversies, it went through bankruptcy proceedings and restructuring, and it has been fighting to remain relevant in an open-source image generation market that has become crowded with capable alternatives. The new funding suggests that investors still see value in Stability AI's IP and open-source brand, even if the company's position has been eroded. Stable Diffusion remains one of the most widely deployed open-source image generation models, embedded in thousands of downstream applications and fine-tuned into countless specialized variants — that installed base has real value even if the company hasn't captured much of it commercially. The $76M raise is modest compared to the hundreds of millions flowing into AI companies with stronger commercial traction, which tells you something about where the market places Stability AI right now. The key question is what the company intends to do with the capital — whether it's investing in next-generation models, commercial partnerships, or just buying time. The open-source image generation space has continued to advance rapidly (with Flux models and others pushing quality higher), so Stability needs a clear differentiation strategy. This feels more like a lifeline than a growth round, but it does keep the company in the game.

stories.title: TikTok to Pay $400M in One of the Largest Child Privacy Settlements in History
stories.summary: TikTok and its parent company ByteDance have agreed to pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit stemming from a 2024 case alleging they collected 'vast amounts of data' on millions of users under the age of 13, in violation of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). This is one of the largest child privacy settlements on record, dwarfing most previous COPPA enforcement actions. The case alleged that TikTok knowingly allowed children under 13 to use the platform without parental consent and collected their data — including location, browsing behavior, and biometric information — without appropriate disclosure or authorization. For ByteDance, $400M is painful but survivable given its scale; the bigger concern is likely the precedent it sets and the regulatory attention it invites. For the broader tech industry, this settlement reinforces that child privacy enforcement is getting more serious and more expensive — other platforms with young user bases should be paying close attention. The settlement comes at an already complicated time for TikTok in the US, which continues to navigate national security-driven legislative pressure around its Chinese ownership. Interestingly, the settlement doesn't require TikTok to admit wrongdoing, which is standard for these agreements but limits its precedential impact in future cases. COPPA was written in 1998 and has been widely criticized as inadequate for the modern algorithmic recommendation environment; this settlement may increase pressure on Congress to update it.

stories.title: X Sends Cease-and-Desist to Open Source Project Nitter Over Alleged Scraping
stories.summary: X (formerly Twitter) has sent cease-and-desist letters to Nitter, the open-source project that provides privacy-friendly front-ends for viewing X content without an account, demanding both its instances and its code repository be taken down. Nitter works by scraping X's public content and presenting it through a cleaner, tracker-free interface — which X characterizes as unauthorized scraping in violation of its terms of service. This move was widely anticipated: X has been aggressively tightening API access and data controls since Elon Musk's acquisition, and Nitter has been in a cat-and-mouse struggle with X's infrastructure changes for years. The Hacker News community is clearly following this closely — both the TechCrunch story and the GitHub issue thread hit the top of the site with over 700 points combined. The legal question is genuinely interesting: scraping publicly accessible content has been the subject of ongoing court battles, with the hiQ v. LinkedIn case establishing that scraping public data is not necessarily a CFAA violation. Whether X's ToS-based claims hold up is a separate question. For the open-source community, the attack on the code repository (not just the running instances) is the more alarming escalation — it suggests X wants to make the software itself unavailable, not just stop specific deployments. Nitter has been particularly important for journalists, researchers, and users in regions where X is partially blocked or inaccessible. This is part of a broader pattern of large platforms attempting to fully enclose their data and eliminate third-party access.

stories.title: Twitch and Amazon Face Lawsuit Over Using Livestreams to Train AI Without Consent
stories.summary: Twitch and its parent company Amazon are facing legal action alleging that they used streamers' video content to train AI models without the creators' permission or compensation. The lawsuit argues that streamers' livestreams constitute original creative works and that using them as AI training data without consent violates creators' rights. This is part of a growing wave of AI training data litigation, but the Twitch case has some distinctive features: the plaintiffs are not professional authors or musicians but content creators whose livelihoods depend on the platform they're suing, which creates a complicated power dynamic. Twitch's Terms of Service grant it broad licenses to use uploaded content, and Amazon will almost certainly argue those licenses cover AI training use — the question is whether courts will agree that such broad ToS grants were ever meaningfully consented to. The case joins a crowded docket of AI training data suits involving The New York Times, Getty Images, and numerous authors, which means the legal landscape here could shift significantly before this case is resolved. For Amazon, the stakes go beyond Twitch: AWS is one of the largest providers of AI infrastructure and has its own AI products, so any adverse ruling about training data could have company-wide implications. For the broader AI industry, how courts handle the consent and compensation questions in these cases will shape what datasets are usable going forward. The creators most affected are likely small and mid-size streamers who have little individual leverage but may benefit from class action consolidation.

stories.title: Measles Deaths in Pennsylvania Highlight Consequences of Declining Vaccination Rates
stories.summary: Two unvaccinated people have died from measles in Pennsylvania, the first measles fatalities in the United States this year, according to state health officials. The deaths are a stark reminder that measles — often thought of as a historical disease in the developed world — remains genuinely dangerous and can kill. Pennsylvania officials noted that many people are simply unfamiliar with the disease and don't understand how severe it can be, which reflects how successful vaccination programs had been at making measles rare before recent declines. The broader context here is deeply concerning: vaccination rates in the US have been declining for several years, driven by vaccine hesitancy movements and, more recently, by political pressure from figures including President Trump to split up the MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) combination vaccine — a proposal that has no scientific basis and that public health experts have warned would reduce uptake. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known — the reproduction number (R0) is estimated between 12 and 18, meaning one infected person can spread it to over a dozen others in an unvaccinated population. Achieving herd immunity requires vaccination rates above 95%, and many US communities have fallen below that threshold. For engineers and tech workers, this story may feel distant, but the information ecosystem that drives vaccine hesitancy — social media recommendation algorithms, AI-generated health misinformation — is directly relevant to the tech industry's responsibilities. This is not a technology story per se, but it's a consequence story about technologies and platforms that have amplified health misinformation at scale.

stories.title: New Bootloader Lets Users Fully De-Meta the Original Meta Quest
stories.summary: A newly released bootloader exploit gives owners of the original Meta Quest headset essentially full control over the device, allowing them to run it entirely independently of Meta's servers and app ecosystem. The technique uses a privilege escalation attack to gain root access, after which users can sideload alternative operating systems and apps without any Meta account or connectivity requirement. This is particularly interesting because the original Quest is several years old and Meta has little financial incentive to maintain it, which means users face the prospect of their hardware becoming bricked by policy or server shutdowns — a real risk that has materialized for other consumer electronics platforms. The right-to-repair and device longevity communities have been pushing back against this kind of planned obsolescence, and a working bootloader is a meaningful technical countermeasure. For the broader AR/VR ecosystem, this also raises questions about what consumers actually own when they buy a device that is fundamentally dependent on manufacturer servers for core functionality. The exploit doesn't appear to require any special hardware modifications — it's a software-level privilege escalation — which means it's accessible to technically sophisticated users without soldering. Meta will almost certainly patch this in newer devices and may push firmware updates that close the vulnerability on older hardware, so the window for using it may be limited. From a security research perspective, the fact that a privilege escalation of this magnitude was possible speaks to the attack surface that always-connected consumer devices present. This is a win for device ownership advocates, even if the practical user base is small.

stories.title: EVE Online Begins Long-Awaited Migration from Stackless Python 2.7 to Python 3
stories.summary: EVE Online, the massively multiplayer space game famous for its extraordinary complexity and scale, has announced it is finally beginning the migration from Stackless Python 2.7 to Python 3 — a technical project that has been discussed for years and that represents one of the most interesting large-scale Python modernization efforts in the industry. The game has been running on Stackless Python (a variant that enables massive concurrency through microthreads) since its launch in 2003, and its last major Python upgrade was 16 years ago. EVE is essentially a single, persistent universe with a complex player-driven economy, political structures, and real-time combat — all running on a Python backend at a scale that very few applications approach. The migration matters to the wider Python community because EVE Online is one of the most compelling case studies of Python at scale, and the lessons from this migration will be genuinely instructive. Stackless Python 3 exists and has been maintained, but migrating a codebase of this age and complexity involves not just syntax changes but behavioral differences in how Python 3 handles strings, bytes, async patterns, and a long list of other things. The EVE engineering team has historically been unusually transparent about their technical challenges, and the migration blog posts will likely be must-reads for engineers working on legacy Python codebases. Simon Willison flagged this as notable, which is generally a reliable signal that the developer community considers it significant. For anyone managing a Python 2 legacy system — and there are still more of them than people admit — this migration will be worth following.

stories.title: Google's Anti-Motion Sickness 'Motion Assist' Feature Begins Rolling Out on Android 17
stories.summary: Google has begun rolling out 'Motion Assist,' its anti-nausea feature for Android 17, initially limited to Pixel devices. The feature works by displaying subtle visual cues — described as dots — that help orient the user's visual field and reduce the perceptual mismatch that causes motion sickness when looking at a screen in a moving vehicle. Motion sickness from screen use is a real and underappreciated accessibility issue; estimates suggest a meaningful portion of the population experiences some degree of discomfort. The fact that Google is shipping a system-level intervention rather than requiring individual apps to implement their own solutions is the right architectural approach — most apps will never bother to implement motion sickness mitigations on their own. The current Pixel-only rollout is typical for Google's staged feature launches; the intent is presumably to gather real-world data before expanding to other Android OEMs. The technical implementation — overlaying subtle visual anchoring cues on top of whatever is being displayed — is interesting because it works at the OS level without requiring any app modifications. Whether it actually works well in practice is an open question; the science on visual motion sickness interventions is real but the efficacy of any specific implementation varies widely. This is a minor story in the grand scheme of things, but it's a good example of the kind of accessibility improvement that tends to get overlooked in launch coverage. Watch for Android OEM adoption timelines and user feedback on real-world effectiveness.

stories.title: New Physics Paper Proposes Black Hole Singularity Is a Surface, Not a Point
stories.summary: A new paper on arXiv is getting significant attention in the physics and Hacker News communities for proposing that black hole singularities — long theorized as infinitely dense points where known physics breaks down — may actually be surfaces rather than zero-dimensional points. If correct, this would be a meaningful revision to the standard model of black hole interiors and might help reconcile some of the mathematical pathologies that arise from point singularities. The paper scored 213 points on Hacker News, suggesting it's resonating with the technically literate community, though arXiv papers haven't been peer-reviewed and should be treated as proposals rather than established results. Singularity theorems — proven by Hawking and Penrose in the 1960s — established that singularities must exist under certain conditions, but they were notably silent on the geometry of those singularities. A surface singularity rather than a point singularity could have interesting implications for information preservation (the black hole information paradox) and for theories of quantum gravity. It's worth being appropriately cautious here: proposals that 'resolve' fundamental problems in theoretical physics circulate regularly and most don't hold up under scrutiny. But the specific claim — about the geometry of singularities rather than their existence — is testable in principle within existing mathematical frameworks, which makes it more tractable than some exotic proposals. For the curious engineer who last thought about black holes in an undergraduate physics class, this is a good excuse to revisit the topic.
